analysis.one_liner: A sweeping energy bill giving federal support and royalty relief to oil, gas, coal, and nuclear producers, with some efficiency and electricity-consumer rules.
analysis.headline: The Senate debated the bill on the floor from May through July 2003 but never held an up-or-down vote; it sat on the Senate calendar when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This was a sprawling rewrite of national energy policy. It cuts the royalties companies pay the government for oil and gas taken from federal lands and offshore waters, speeds up permits for drilling on public lands, sets up federal loan guarantees for an Alaska natural gas pipeline, extends the government's liability cap for nuclear accidents, and repeals a 1935 law that regulated utility holding companies. It also raises efficiency standards for buildings and appliances, funds low-income weatherization and appliance rebates, adds penalties for manipulating electricity markets, and requires utilities to offer net metering and protections against Slamming and Cramming.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, oil and gas companies on federal leases would pay reduced royalties in weak markets and on deepwater and Alaskan offshore production; coal companies could lease far larger federal tracts; nuclear developers would get extended accident-liability protection and federal financing help; utility holding companies would be freed from 1935-era regulation; and an Alaska pipeline consortium would get loan guarantees, a fast-track regulatory clock, and a coordinator empowered to strip conditions from federal approvals. Households would get appliance rebates, low-income efficiency grants, tougher efficiency standards, and clearer, better-policed retail electricity markets.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil, gas, coal, nuclear, and utility holding companies

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the royalty rate to as low as 5% for marginal federal oil and gas wells when prices fall, and suspends royalties on 5 to 12 million barrels of oil equivalent per lease for new deepwater Gulf of Mexico leases and on Alaska offshore planning areas.
Repeals the 160-acre limit on federal coal leases and modifies mining-plan and advance-royalty rules, letting coal companies control far larger federal tracts.

Extends the Price-Anderson nuclear accident liability framework, authorizes the Energy Secretary to supplement private financing for new nuclear plants, and raises ceilings on federal uranium sales from 3 million to 10 million pounds per year.

Sets mandatory reliability standards for the bulk power system, requires FERC to create public price-transparency rules, bans false price reporting and round-trip trading, and increases civil and criminal penalties for market manipulation.

Revises appliance and consumer-product efficiency standards, upgrades federal building efficiency requirements, funds a low-income community energy efficiency pilot, appliance rebate programs, and public housing conservation measures.
Requires utilities to offer net metering and time-based metering on request and to give distributed generation access to the local grid.
Allows the Energy Secretary to grant a preference in selling federal royalty oil to support federal low-income energy assistance programs.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers bear the cost of royalty relief on federal and offshore oil and gas, the risk on Alaska pipeline loan guarantees, and the bill's authorized appropriations for clean coal, nuclear, hydrogen, and renewable programs. Members of the public near federal drilling would face faster permitting with less time for environmental review. Utility customers lose the 1935 Holding Company Act's structural limits on utility empires, and the extended nuclear liability cap leaves taxpayers exposed above the industry-funded amount if a serious accident occurs.

drawbacks.text: The royalty relief provisions directly reduce money the federal government collects from oil and gas taken from public lands and waters, including automatic suspensions of royalties worth millions of barrels on new deepwater Gulf leases and Alaska offshore production.

The Alaska pipeline subtitle instructs regulators to presume a public need for the project, requires a decision within 60 days of the final environmental statement, lets a federal coordinator bar agency conditions that might slow construction, and channels all court challenges to a single appeals court — while taxpayers back the project with loan guarantees.

It repeals the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935, the law that broke up the utility trusts of the 1930s, replacing it only with requirements that federal and state regulators be given access to company books and records.

Extending Price-Anderson keeps the ceiling on what nuclear operators must pay after a severe accident, leaving costs above that level to the public; a good-faith supporter would note the industry argues the cap keeps insurance available at all.

The permitting subtitle directs 'expeditious compliance' with the National Environmental Policy Act for drilling applications and creates a permit-streamlining pilot on six Bureau of Land Management field offices, shortening the review that local communities and surface owners currently get.
Section 972 authorizes a $125 million federal loan to the owner of a single experimental coal plant built under a 1991 DOE cooperative agreement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The efficiency, reliability, and consumer-protection provisions are real and would have helped households, especially after the bill's reliability title addressed the kind of grid failures that caused the August 2003 blackout. But the bill's largest and most permanent provisions run the other way: reduced royalties on public resources, expanded federal coal leasing, nuclear liability protection and financing help, pipeline loan guarantees, and repeal of the utility holding company law. On balance the structure tilts toward established energy producers, with consumer benefits attached around the edges.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate spent three months debating the bill on the floor, leadership tried and then abandoned a procedural move to send it back to the Energy Committee with instructions, and it was returned to the calendar and never brought to a final vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Pete Domenici, chairman of the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, introduced S. 14 on April 30, 2003 with no cosponsors.
The bill was considered on the Senate floor on roughly 25 days between May 6 and July 31, 2003, a stretch of extended debate unusual for a bill that had not gone through committee.

On July 30, 2003, Majority Leader Bill Frist moved to commit the bill back to the Energy Committee with instructions to report it back immediately with an amendment, and presented a cloture motion — a vote requiring 60 senators to cut off debate — on that motion.
The next day the cloture motion and the motion to commit were withdrawn by unanimous consent, and the bill was returned to the Senate calendar, Calendar No. 79.
No final passage vote or recorded vote on the bill ever occurred, and the bill remained on the calendar when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the Treasury kept collecting full royalties on federal and offshore oil and gas for another two years and utility holding companies stayed under the 1935 law a little longer. The relief was temporary: Congress passed a closely related successor, the Energy Policy Act of 2005, that restored many of the same industry provisions, so energy producers ultimately gained anyway while consumers waited two years for the efficiency and reliability rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Energy industries, once a similar 2005 law passed

for.name: Sen. Pete Domenici
for.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, the Senate's comprehensive energy package, and put it straight onto the calendar without a committee markup.

for.name: Sen. Bill Frist
for.what_they_did: Moved to commit the bill to the Energy Committee with instructions to report back immediately with an amendment, and presented a cloture motion to force the issue; withdrew both when no agreement could be reached.

against.name: Tom Daschle
against.what_they_did: Demanded votes on Democratic priorities including a renewable fuels mandate and climate provisions during the floor debate; without agreement on which amendments would get votes, the bill could not advance to a final vote.

against.name: Sens. John McCain and Joseph Lieberman
against.role: Senate sponsors of a mandatory greenhouse gas cap amendment
against.what_they_did: Sought a floor vote on their climate amendment during consideration of the energy bill; the leadership did not allow the vote, and the standoff contributed to the bill stalling.

sides.party_line_note: No recorded vote was ever taken on S. 14 — the only vote-like action, a cloture motion, was withdrawn by unanimous consent — so the record shows no party split, and the bill's sponsor had no cosponsors at all.

industries.note: The bill cuts royalty rates on marginal wells, suspends royalties on new deepwater Gulf and Alaska offshore production, lifts federal lease acreage limits, and speeds drilling permits on public lands. The value comes out of royalties owed to the federal treasury on public resources.

Repealing the 160-acre federal coal lease limit and easing mining-plan and royalty rules lets companies consolidate much larger federal tracts, while taxpayers fund the Clean Coal Power Initiative. Communities near expanded mining bear the surface impacts.

The bill extends Price-Anderson liability protection, provides federal financing support for new plants, and raises uranium sales ceilings. Accident costs above the industry-funded cap fall on the public.

Repealing the 1935 Holding Company Act frees utility empires from structural limits and SEC-era oversight, while the bill imposes reliability standards, net metering obligations, market-manipulation penalties, and slamming and cramming rules on the industry.

The bill offers federal loan guarantees, a 60-day regulatory decision deadline, a presumption of public need, and a coordinator who can strip conditions from federal approvals, shifting project risk onto taxpayers for a private pipeline.

Production incentive payments, expanded geothermal leasing, net metering access, and renewable R&D appropriations flow to wind, solar, geothermal, and biomass developers. Households gain alongside through cheaper efficient appliances and rebates.
The bill funds a low-income community efficiency pilot, appliance rebates, public housing energy improvements, and a royalty preference that can feed the federal low-income energy assistance program.
